## Appendix A From the Schwarzian action to the Liouville action

The JT gravity action can be written as [4, 3, 5]

$$ I=-{1\over 4\pi}\left[\int\phi(R+2)+2\phi_{b}\int K\right]\longrightarrow-{\phi_{b}\over 2\pi}\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\tau\{f,\tau\} $$

where $\phi$ is normalized so that the entropy is given just by $S=\phi_{h}$ where $\phi_{h}$ is the value at the horizon. The arrow in the right hand side means that if we take $\phi_{b}$ large and we go near the boundary, then the action reduces to the Schwarzian expression where $\tau$ is the proper time near the boundary. It is sometimes customary to defined a rescaled version of these $\phi_{b}={\phi_{r}\over\epsilon}$ , $t=\epsilon\tau$ that remains constant as we take the boundary limit with $\epsilon\to 0$ . We could also do the further rescaling $u={\pi\over\phi_{r}}t$ which sets the coefficient of the Schwarzian to a half

$$ I=-{1\over 2}\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u\{f,u\}=\int{1\over 4}\dot{\ell}^{2}+\pi_{f}(e^{-\ell}-f^{\prime}) $$

A simple way to connect the parameter $\phi_{r}$ to the parameters of black holes is to compute their near extremal entropy as a function of the inverse temperature and compare with

$$ S-S_{0}={2\pi\phi_{r}\over\beta} $$

For example, for the four dimensional Reissner Nordstrom black hole we have

$$ S-S_{e}={4\pi\over 4G_{N}}(r_{+}^{2}-r_{+}r_{-})=S_{e}{4\pi r_{e}\over\beta}~,~~~~~~\beta=4\pi{r_{+}^{2}\over(r_{+}-r_{-})}~,~~~~~~r_{+}-r_{-}\ll r_{+} $$

so that $\phi_{r}=2S_{e}r_{e}$ , where $r_{e}$ is the extremal radius, $r_{e}^{2}=r_{+}r_{-}$ .

In these variables, we can think of the three SL(2) generators as

$$ L_{-}=-\partial_{f}~,~~~~L_{0}=-f\partial_{f}+\partial_{\ell}~,~~~~L_{+}=-f^{2}\partial_{f}+2f\partial_{\ell}-e^{-\ell} $$

where $\pi_{f}$ is the momentum conjugate to $f$ and $\pi_{\ell}$ the momentum conjugate to $\ell$ .

When we consider the TFD, it is convenient to choose a new variable $\tilde{f}=1/f$ , $\tilde{\ell}=\ell+2\log x$ related via an SL(2) transformation. This can be used to describe the left particle, we also used that $\tilde{\gamma}=\gamma-e^{-\ell}/f$ and implicitly assumed that the last term in (196) has a $\partial_{\gamma}$ acting on a wavefunction with an $e^{\gamma}$ dependence, $e^{-\ell}\to e^{-\ell}\partial_{\gamma}$ . We can then express $L_{a}$ in terms of $\tilde{f}$ .

$$ L^{l}_{-}={\tilde{f}}^{2}\partial_{\tilde{f}}-2{\tilde{f}}\partial_{\tilde{\ell}}-e^{-\tilde{\ell}}~,~~~~L^{l}_{0}={\tilde{f}}\partial_{\tilde{f}}-\partial_{\tilde{\ell}}~,~~~~L^{l}_{+}=\partial_{\tilde{f}} $$

We then make a gauge choice where we set $\tilde{f}_{l}=0$ and $\tilde{f}^{\prime}_{l}=1$ . In addition, we make the choice $f_{r}=0$ , but no condition on $f^{\prime}_{r}$ . The renormalized distance is then1919 19 This comes from the formula $\cosh d=-Y_{1}.Y_{2}={(t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}+z_{1}^{2}+z_{2}^{2}\over 2z_{1}z_{2}}$ and we have rescaled $z\to\epsilon z$ .

$$ e^{d}\sim{(t_{1}-t_{2})^{2}\over z_{1}z_{2}}~~~\longrightarrow~~~~e^{-\ell}={f_{l}^{\prime}f_{r}^{\prime}\over(f_{l}-f_{r})^{2}}={\tilde{f}_{l}^{\prime}f_{r}^{\prime}\over(1-\tilde{f}_{l}f_{r})^{2}}\to f^{\prime}_{r} $$

where $d=\ell-2\log\epsilon$ , with $\epsilon$ as discussed after (192).

In addition, we have that the $L_{-}^{l}$ expression becomes

$$ L_{-}^{l}=-1 $$

and the gauge constraint $L^{l}_{-}+L^{r}_{-}=0$ implies that $\pi=1$ . Then the Lagrangian then becomes (in Euclidean time)

$$ I=\int{1\over 4}\dot{\ell}^{2}+e^{-\ell} $$

which is what we used in (2). We can view the other constraints as determining the $\tilde{\ell}$ and $\tilde{f}$ dependence away from the point $\tilde{\ell}=\tilde{f}=0$ .

## Appendix B Away from the Schwarzian limit for the bosonic case

The description of the boundary gravitational mode in terms of an SL(2)/U(1) quotient was discussed in [10, 11, 39]. Here we just mention a few points about the form of the problem away from the Schwarzian limit.

Let us first review the case of $H_{2}$ space. Then we can write $g\in$ SL(2) as

$$ g=e^{i\phi\sigma_{2}/2}e^{\sigma_{3}\rho/2}e^{i\chi\sigma_{2}/2} $$

Then the left invariant forms can be defined as

$$ \displaystyle g^{-1}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}g \displaystyle= \displaystyle{1\over 2}w_{a}\sigma^{a}={1\over 2}\left[e^{-i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}e^{-\sigma_{3}\rho/2}i\sigma_{2}e^{\sigma_{3}\rho/2}e^{i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi+e^{-i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}\sigma_{3}e^{i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho+i\sigma_{2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\chi\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle{1\over 2}\left[i\sigma_{2}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\chi+\cosh\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi)+e^{-i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\,\sigma_{3}-\sinh\rho\,\sigma_{1}\!\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi)e^{i\chi\sigma_{2}/2}\right] $$

We quotient under the action $g\to ge^{i\alpha\sigma_{2}}$ . This breaks the right SL(2) symmetry to U(1). This shifts the $\chi$ coordinate, $\chi\to\chi+$ constant. The left SL(2) symmetry remains and will be the isometries of $H_{2}$ . This gives the usual left invariant forms

$$ w_{2}=i(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\chi+\cosh\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi)~,~~~~w_{1}=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\sin\chi-\sinh\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi\cos\chi~,~~~~~~w_{3}=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\cos\chi+\sinh\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi\sin\chi $$

The metric in hyperbolic space is simply

$$ w_{1}^{2}+w_{3}^{2}\propto\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho^{2}+\sinh^{2}\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\phi^{2} $$

which is invariant under the qoutient group, as expected. Because of this reason we do not need to calculate the full $\chi$ dependence of the $w_{i}$ to get the metric (205). We can then write an invariant action of the form

$$ S=\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t{1\over 2}(w_{1}^{2}+w_{3}^{2})+\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}tqi(w_{2}-iA)=\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t{1\over 2}(\dot{\rho}^{2}+\sinh^{2}\rho\dot{\phi}^{2})-q\int\cosh\rho\dot{\phi} $$

where we have added a term involving $w_{2}-A$ where $A$ is the gauge field. We choose the gauge $\chi=0$ and integrate out $A$ . In the end, a term like $iq(w_{2}-A)$ give us the magnetic-like coupling for the particle moving on $H_{2}$ .

This action, (206), is also equivalent to starting with the full naive $G\times G$ invariant action and gauging the quotient group. The charge of the magnetic field coupling is imaginary. The reasonable coupling to the magnetic field would be one where $q$ is imaginary. However in our problem q is real [10, 11]. We can take the large $q$ limit, rescaling also $\rho$ as $e^{\rho}=qe^{\tilde{\rho}}$ . Then the first term combines with the magnetic field coupling to get

$$ {1\over 2}q^{2}({1\over 2}e^{\tilde{\rho}}\dot{\phi}-1)^{2}-{1\over 2}q^{2} $$

The last term is a constant that we can neglect. The first term imposes that $e^{-\tilde{\rho}}=\dot{\phi}/2$ . We can then now substitute this back into the remaining terms of (206) to obtain

$$ \int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t{1\over 2}\left[\dot{\tilde{\rho}}^{2}-\dot{\phi}^{2}\right]=\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t{1\over 2}\left[\left({\ddot{\phi}\over\dot{\phi}}\right)^{2}-\dot{\phi}^{2}\right]=-\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}t\{\tan{\phi\over 2},t\} $$

where we have neglected some total derivatives. So we see that we get the usual Schwarzian action.

The wavefunctions can be viewed as representations where we diagonalize the right factor. In other words, we can consider

$$ \Psi_{j,m,q}(\rho,\phi)=\langle jm|g(\rho,\phi)|j,q\rangle $$

where we have removed the right most factor in $g$ (201). For more details see [10, 11].

### B.1 Generators

It is useful to write the generators of $SL(2)$ . These are obtained by acting with an SL(2) generator on $g$ and then writing the answer as $g(x+\delta x)$ where $x=(\phi,\rho,\chi)$ . In this way we get

$$ \displaystyle i\sigma_{2}/2 \displaystyle\to \displaystyle\partial_{\phi} \displaystyle\sigma_{3}/2 \displaystyle\to \displaystyle-{\sin\phi\over\tanh\rho}\partial_{\phi}+{\sin\phi\over\sinh\rho}\partial_{\chi}+\cos\phi\partial_{\rho} \displaystyle\sigma_{1}/2 \displaystyle\to \displaystyle-{\cos\phi\over\tanh\rho}\partial_{\phi}+{\cos\phi\over\sinh\rho}\partial_{\chi}-\sin\phi\partial_{\rho} $$

The quotient is obtained by setting $\partial_{\chi}=q$ . But now we could construct the Casimir which gives

$$ C_{2}\sim\partial_{\rho}^{2}+{1\over\tanh\rho}\partial_{\rho}+{1\over\sinh^{2}\rho}(\partial_{\phi}-\cosh\rho\partial_{\chi})^{2}-\partial_{\chi}^{2} $$

We can then identify this with the energy. This is the problem away from the Schwarzian limit [10, 11], we can then further take the large $q$ limit to obtain the Schwarzian limit.

## Appendix C $\mathcal{N}=1$ correlators

In this section we discuss some aspects about the ${\cal N}=1$ super-Schwarzian theory. This case was analyzed in depth in [13] to whom we refer for further details (our conventions are slightly different). Here we will work out the boundary particle propagator.

We now have the supergroup $OSp(1|2)$ whose algebra is

$$ \begin{split}[L_{m},L_{n}]=(m-n)L_{m+n}\\
\{G_{r},G_{s}\}=2L_{r+s}\\
[L_{m},G_{r}]=\left(\frac{m}{2}-r\right)G_{m+r}\end{split} $$

We can introduce coordinates $x,\rho,\gamma,\theta_{\pm}$ associated to each of the five generators. Writing the group element as

$$ g=e^{-xL_{-}}e^{\theta_{-}G_{-}}e^{\rho L_{0}}e^{\theta_{+}G_{+}}e^{\gamma L_{+}} $$

we get the following expressions for the left generators

$$ \begin{split}{\cal L}_{-}&=-\partial_{x},\\
{\cal L}_{0}&=-x\partial_{x}+\partial_{\rho}-{1\over 2}\theta_{-}\partial_{\theta_{-}}\\
{\cal L}_{+}&=e^{-\rho}\partial_{\gamma}-x^{2}\partial_{x}+x\left(2\partial_{\rho}-\theta_{-}\partial_{\theta_{-}}\right)-e^{-\rho/2}\theta_{-}D_{+}\\
{\cal G}_{+}&=e^{-\rho/2}D_{+}+x(\partial_{\theta_{-}}-\theta_{-}\partial_{x})+2\theta_{-}\partial_{\rho}\\
{\cal G}_{-}&=\partial_{\theta_{-}}-{\theta}_{-}\partial_{x}\\
&~{\rm with}~~~~D_{+}=\partial_{\theta_{+}}+\theta_{+}\partial_{\gamma}\end{split} $$

We also have the right generators

$$ {\cal L}^{R}_{+}=\partial_{\gamma}~,~~~~~~~~~~{\cal G}_{+}^{R}=\partial_{\theta_{+}}-\theta_{+}\partial_{\gamma}~,~~~~~~~~~~~~~\{{\cal G}_{+}^{R},{\cal G}_{+}^{R}\}=-2{\cal L}^{R}_{+} $$

and the Casimir

$$ \displaystyle{\cal C} \displaystyle= \displaystyle L_{0}^{2}-{1\over 2}(L_{+}L_{-}+L_{-}L_{+})-{1\over 4}[G_{-},G_{+}] \displaystyle{\cal C} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\partial_{\rho}^{2}+{1\over 2}\partial_{\rho}+e^{-\rho}\partial_{x}\partial_{\gamma}-{1\over 2}e^{-\rho/2}D_{-}D_{+}~,~~~~~~~~~~D_{-}=\partial_{\theta_{-}}+\theta_{-}\partial_{x} $$

The spacetime supercharge is

$$ \displaystyle Q \displaystyle= \displaystyle(\partial_{\rho}+{1\over 4})D_{+}-e^{-\rho/2}\partial_{\gamma}D_{-} $$

which obeys $Q^{2}=\partial_{\gamma}({\cal C}+{1\over 16})$ . We can define the Hamiltonian to be $H=-({\cal C}+{1\over 16})$ .

An interesting fact about the OSp( $1|2$ ) algebra is that there is a superCasimir or sCasimir element $\mathcal{Q}=G^{-}G^{+}-G^{+}G^{-}+1/8$ which is Grassmann-even, commutes with all the bosonic generators, but anti-commutes with all the fermionic elements. There is a simple relation between the right sCasimir and the supercharge:

$$ \begin{split}Q=4\mathcal{Q}^{R}\mathcal{G}^{R}_{+}\end{split} $$

Note that this definition of $Q$ is manifestly left-invariant. In addition this notation makes it clear that $Q$ anti-commutes with $\mathcal{G}_{+}^{R}$ .

### C.1 Invariants

Here we record the form of invariants of two coordinates

$$ \displaystyle w \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{\rho_{1}/2+\rho_{2}/2}(x_{1}-x_{2}-\theta_{1-}\theta_{2-}) \displaystyle\eta_{1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\theta_{1+}-{e^{\rho_{2}/2}(\theta_{1-}-\theta_{2-})\over w} \displaystyle\eta_{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\theta_{2+}-{e^{\rho_{1}/2}(\theta_{1-}-\theta_{2-})\over w} \displaystyle\Phi \displaystyle= \displaystyle\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{2}+{e^{(\rho_{1}-\rho_{2})/2}+e^{-(\rho_{1}-\rho_{2})/2}\over w}+{(\theta_{1-}-\theta_{2-})(-e^{\rho_{2}/2}\theta_{1+}+e^{\rho_{1}/2}\theta_{2+})\over w} $$

We can write the supercharge in terms of invariants

$$ Q_{1}={1\over 2}(w\partial_{w}+{1\over 2})(\partial_{\eta_{1}}+\eta_{1}\partial_{\Phi})+{1\over w}\partial_{\Phi}(\partial_{\eta_{2}}-\eta_{2}\partial_{\Phi}) $$

We can also write the right supersymmetries in terms of invariants

$$ {\cal G}^{R}_{+1}=\partial_{\eta_{1}}-\eta_{1}\partial_{\Phi}~,~~~~~~~~~~~{\cal G}^{R}_{+2}=\partial_{\eta_{2}}+\eta_{2}\partial_{\Phi} $$

which anticommute with the supercharge. Note that we can interpret these as extra fermions which do not appear in the Liouville description, which can be interpreted as the terms in parenthesis in (227). We could remove this extra degree of freedom by imposing a condition of the form

$$ ({\cal G}^{R}_{1}+{\cal G}^{R}_{2})P=0 $$

This condition removes the extra unwanted fermionic degrees of freedom2020 20 Imposing $\mathcal{G}_{+1}^{R}+\mathcal{G}_{+2}^{R}=0$ is equivalent to imposing that $\mathcal{G}^{R}$ commutes with the propagator $e^{-uH}$ . We could also consider $\mathcal{G}_{+1}^{R}-\mathcal{G}_{+2}^{R}=0$ , which would impose that $\mathcal{G}^{R}$ anti-commutes with the propagator. This would be incorrect since the propagator is bosonic. . Note that the operator in the left hand side squares to zero when acting on the propagator that is annihilated by ${\cal L}_{1+}^{R}+{\cal L}_{2+}^{R}$ , due to

$$ {\cal L}_{1}^{R}P=-{\cal L}_{2}^{R}P=-\mathfrak{q}P $$

Note that we can “improve” the invariants by defining

$$ \begin{split}\tilde{\Phi}=\Phi-\eta_{1}\eta_{2},\quad\tilde{\eta}=\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}\end{split} $$

Together with $w$ , we have three invariants are annihilated by $\mathcal{G}_{+1}^{R}+\mathcal{G}_{+2}^{R}$ .

### C.2 Propagator

Here we will compute the propagator for arbitrary times. In writing the propagator, it is convenient to think in terms of a worldline superspace propagator

$$ P=\langle 1|e^{\kappa_{1}Q}e^{-(u_{1}-u_{2})H}e^{-\kappa_{2}Q}|2\rangle=e^{-(u_{12}-\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2})H}e^{(\kappa_{1}-\kappa_{2})Q}~,~~~~~~~{\rm with}~~~Q^{2}=H $$

where $\kappa_{i}$ are the superspace coordinates of the worldline theory. We define the covariant derivatives $D_{\kappa}=\partial_{\kappa}+\kappa\partial_{u}$ . Note that the propagator can depend only on the combinations $\kappa_{1}-\kappa_{2}$ and $U=u_{1}-u_{2}-\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}$ . We can view this as a consequence of worldline supersymmetry2121 21 These combinations are annihilated by $\tilde{Q}_{1}+\tilde{Q}_{2}$ with $\tilde{Q}=\partial_{\kappa}-\kappa\partial_{u}$ being the combination that anticommutes with $D_{\kappa}$ .. In addition we see that we have that $Q_{1}P=D_{\kappa_{1}}P$ . When we compose the propagator as in $P(1,2)P(2,3)$ we do not integrate over $\kappa_{2}$ (as we do not integrate over $u_{2}$ ), we expect that the result should be independent of it.

We now make an ansatz for the propagator which is a parity even function of the invariants of the form

$$ \hat{P}=e^{-\mathfrak{q}\tilde{\Phi}}\left[A+(\kappa_{1}-\kappa_{2})\tilde{\eta}C\right]=e^{-\mathfrak{q}\Phi}\left[(1+\mathfrak{q}\eta_{1}\eta_{2})A+(\kappa_{1}-\kappa_{2})(\eta_{1}-\eta_{2})C\right] $$

This ansatz is manifestly invariant under $\mathcal{G}_{+1}^{R}+\mathcal{G}_{+2}^{R}$ as well as all the left generators.

We now impose the equation

$$ Q_{1}\hat{P}={\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}}D_{\kappa_{1}}\hat{P} $$

where the factor of $\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}$ arises due to the normalization of $Q_{1}$ in (227)2222 22 As discussed after (221) we get $Q^{2}=\mathfrak{q}H$ . . This results in the conditions

$$ Q_{1}(1+\mathfrak{q}\eta_{1}\eta_{2})A=\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}(\eta_{1}-\eta_{2})C~,~~~~~~Q_{1}(\eta_{1}-\eta_{2})C=-\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}\partial_{U}(1+\mathfrak{q}\eta_{1}\eta_{2})A=\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}E(1+\mathfrak{q}\eta_{1}\eta_{2})A $$

where we assumed that we are in the subsector of energy $E$ . Using the form of the supercharge (227), we find that (235) implies

$$ C={\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}\over 2}\left[yA^{\prime}(y)+(y-{1\over 2})A(y)\right]~,~~~~~~~y={2\mathfrak{q}\over w} $$

and an equation for $A$ which is solved by

$$ A(y)=y\left[K_{{1\over 2}+i2s}(y)+K_{{1\over 2}-i2s}(y)\right]=\sqrt{y}\Psi_{+}(y)~,~~~~y={2\mathfrak{q}\over w}~,~~~~~E=s^{2} $$

where we also defined the function $\Psi_{+}$ which is related to a super-Liouville wavefunction as we will review below. In summary, the final form of the propagator for fixed energy is (233) with $A$ in (237) and $C_{1}$ in (236). In addition, we need to integrate over energy to find the fixed $u$ propagator. In principle, that measure factor is determined by demanding the composition law of the propagators. In practice, we can determine it by comparing to the Liouville results in [17].

The integral over each point involves the measure

$$ \int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu=\int{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\,e^{\rho/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{-}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{+}} $$

where the factor of $e^{\rho/2}$ is fixed by scaling. Note that $\theta_{+}$ is neutral under scaling (217).

General correlators are given by

$$ \displaystyle\langle O_{1}(u_{1},\kappa_{1})\cdots O(u_{n},\kappa_{n})\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle\int{\prod_{i}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{i}\over{\rm vol}(OSp(1|2))}\hat{P}(1,2)\hat{P}(2,3)\cdots\hat{P}(n,1)\times \displaystyle~~~~\times\prod_{i}e^{-\Delta_{i}\rho_{i}}\langle O(x_{1},\theta_{1-})\cdots O(x_{n},\theta_{n-})\rangle $$

where the last factor include the expected form of the correlator of bulk fields when we take them near the boundary.

### C.3 Recovering the Liouville two point functions

As a check of this result, we recover the two point functions that were computed in [17] using the Liouville method. In the Liouville method one starts for a superliouville quantum mechanics which is the dimensional reduction of a theory in $1+1$ dimensions with $(1,1)$ supersymmetry. The variables are the wormhole length, $\ell$ , and two fermionic partners arising from the action of the supersymmetry acting on the left and the right sides. We will not give the explicit form of the Lagrangian, which can be found in section 6 of [40]. We mention that we have two wavefunctions whose bosonic components have the form

$$ \Psi_{s,\pm}(\ell)=e^{-\ell/4}\left[K_{{1\over 2}+2is}(2e^{-\ell/2})\pm K_{{1\over 2}-2is}(2e^{-\ell/2})\right] $$

And the correlation functions have the form

$$ \langle E^{\prime}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|E\rangle\propto\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\ell\Psi_{s^{\prime},+}(\ell)e^{-\Delta\ell}\Psi_{s,+}(\ell)~,~~~~~~~~~~E=s^{2} $$

Now we will recover this from our propagator and (240) for $n=2$ . First, we choose the gauge conditions

$$ x_{1}=1~,~~~~x_{2}=0,~~~\rho_{2}=0~,~~~~\theta_{1-}=\theta_{2-}=0~,~~~~~ $$

which implies that

$$ w=e^{\ell\over 2},~~~~~~\ell=\rho_{1}~,~~~~~~\eta_{1}=\theta_{1+}~,~~~~~~~\eta_{2}=\theta_{2+} $$

whose Jacobian is trivial. We also set $\kappa_{1}=\kappa_{2}=0$ for simplicity. Then the two point function becomes

$$ \int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\ell e^{\ell/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{1+}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{2+}e^{-\ell\Delta}\hat{P}(1,2)\hat{P}(2,1) $$

The phase factor $\Phi$ cancels in this expression. We also set $\mathfrak{q}=1$ . After doing the $\theta_{+}$ integrals we get something proportional to

$$ \int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\ell e^{\ell/2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{1+}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{2+}e^{-\ell\Delta}A_{s^{\prime}}(y)A_{s}(y)~,~~~~~~~~~y=2e^{-\ell/2} $$

which agrees with (242) after we use (237). Notice that the extra factor of $\sqrt{y}$ in (237) cancels agains the extra measure factor in (246).

Of course, the full two point function in time also involves and integral over the energies with the appropriate $\rho(E)\rho(E^{\prime})e^{-u^{\prime}E^{\prime}-uE}$ factors.

## Appendix E Computing the matrix elements

In this appendix, we compute matrix elements of various operators in the super-Liouville quantum mechanics.

### E.1 BPS operators

First we consider a matrix element of the state $|F^{+}\rangle$ . The integral involved is the same as for the case with no supersymmetry [17] and we get

$$ \langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle={\sqrt{E^{\prime}E}\over\pi}{\Gamma(\Delta\pm is\pm is^{\prime})\over\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-2\Delta} $$

Now, in order to compute the other matrix elements we use that the other wavefunctions are given by

$$ |H_{s,j}\rangle={1\over\sqrt{E}}\bar{Q}_{l}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle~,~~~~~|L_{s,j}\rangle={1\over\sqrt{E}}i\bar{Q}_{r}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle $$

In addition, we can use commutation relations

$$ [\bar{Q}_{r},e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}]=[Q_{l},e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}]=0 $$

This then leads to a simple evaluation of the matrix elements among $H$ or among $L$ . In those cases we commute either the $\bar{Q}_{r}$ or the $Q_{l}$ . For example, for

$$ \displaystyle\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|H_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle{1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|Q_{l}e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}\bar{Q}_{l}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle={1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}Q_{l}\bar{Q}_{l}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle= \displaystyle= \displaystyle{1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}E\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|F_{s,j}^{+}\rangle={E\over\pi}{\Gamma(\Delta\pm is\pm is^{\prime})\over\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-1} $$

We can do the same for the $|L\rangle$ states and we get a similar answer, except that now we move the $\bar{Q}_{r}$ to the left side so we get a factor of $E^{\prime}$ rather than $E$ . In this way we can also see that

$$ \langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|L_{s,j}\rangle=0 $$

by commuting the $Q_{l}$ from the left side to the right side For the case

$$ \displaystyle\langle L_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|H_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle-i{1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|Q_{r}e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}\bar{Q}_{l}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle= \displaystyle= \displaystyle-i{1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|\{[Q_{r},e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}],\bar{Q}_{l}\}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle-i{1\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|(2i\Delta e^{-\ell/2+ia}+4\Delta^{2}\psi_{r}\bar{\psi}_{l})e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle{2\Delta\over\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-(\Delta+{1\over 2})\ell-ia(2\Delta-1))}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle= \displaystyle{2\Delta\over\pi}{\Gamma(\Delta+{1\over 2}\pm is\pm is^{\prime})\over\Gamma(2(\Delta+{1\over 2}))}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-2\Delta+1} $$

where we used that the operators annihilate the appropriate state to write it just as some commutators and anticommutators of the operator in question.

When we want to consider the zero energy states $Z_{j}$ , then it is convenient to obtain these from limits of $|H\rangle$ as $s\to{i\over 2}(j-1/2)$ . And it is convenient to start with the matrix elements in (263) which do not involve explicit factors of $E$ that are going to zero. So, starting for $\langle L|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|H\rangle$ and taking the limit, we get the matrix element $\langle L|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|Z\rangle$ . Similarly, we could start with $\langle H|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|H\rangle$ and take the limit on the $H$ on the left, setting $s^{\prime}=\pm{i\over 2}(j-{1\over 2})$ to obtain the $\langle Z|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|H\rangle$ matrix element. Further talking a limit of this one we get the $\langle Z|e^{-\Delta(\ell+2ia)}|Z\rangle$ matrix element.

### E.2 Neutral operators

The process for the neutral operator works similarly. We use the fact that each time we use commutator relations, we have two choices for which way to move an operator. We can do the calculation by averaging over these two choices. The basic matrix element needed is

$$ \displaystyle\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle={\sqrt{E^{\prime}E}\over\pi}{\Gamma(\Delta\pm is\pm is^{\prime})\over\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j,j^{\prime}} $$

It is useful to keep this property in mind:

$$ \displaystyle\{A,BC\}=B\{A,C\}+[A,B]C $$

Using this relation, we can derive

$$ \displaystyle\{Q_{l},[e^{-\Delta\ell},\bar{Q}_{l}]\}+\{[Q_{l},e^{-\Delta\ell}],\bar{Q}_{l}\} \displaystyle=i\Delta e^{-\Delta\ell}\left(-i\partial_{a}+\Delta[\psi_{l},\bar{\psi}_{l}]\right) \displaystyle\{Q_{r},[e^{-\Delta\ell},\bar{Q}_{r}]\}+\{[Q_{r},e^{-\Delta\ell}],\bar{Q}_{r}\} \displaystyle=i\Delta e^{-\Delta\ell}\left(i\partial_{a}+\Delta[\psi_{r},\bar{\psi}_{r}]\right) \displaystyle\{Q_{l},[e^{-\Delta\ell},\bar{Q}_{r}]\} \displaystyle=-i\Delta e^{-\ell\Delta}\left(e^{-\frac{\ell}{2}-ia}-i\Delta\psi_{l}\bar{\psi}_{r}\right) $$

We first compute $\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|H_{s,j}\rangle$ :

$$ \displaystyle 2\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|H_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{2}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|Q_{l}e^{-\Delta\ell}\bar{Q}_{l}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{E+E^{\prime}}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle+\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|\{Q_{l},[e^{-\Delta\ell},\bar{Q}_{l}]\}+\{[Q_{l},e^{-\Delta\ell}],\bar{Q}_{l}\}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle $$

Finally, since $\partial_{a}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle=i(j-\frac{1}{2})$ , we obtain:

$$ \displaystyle\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|H_{s,j}\rangle={1\over 2\pi}(E+E^{\prime}+\Delta(\Delta+j-\frac{1}{2})\frac{\Gamma(\Delta\pm is\pm is^{\prime})}{\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j,j^{\prime}} $$

The matrix elements $\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|Z_{j}\rangle,\langle Z_{j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|H_{s,j}\rangle,\langle Z_{j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|Z_{j}\rangle$ follow from (275) by taking the limit $s\to\frac{i}{2}(j-\frac{1}{2})$ for the appropriate state. Computing $\langle L_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|L_{s,j}\rangle$ using (271) we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\langle L_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|L_{s,j}\rangle={1\over 2\pi}\left(E+E^{\prime}+\Delta(\Delta-j+\frac{1}{2})\right)\frac{\Gamma(\Delta\pm is\pm is^{\prime})}{\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j,j^{\prime}} $$

Finally, to compute the mixed matrix elements, we use (272) and the fact that $F^{+}$ state is annihilated by $Q_{r},Q_{l}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\langle H_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\Delta\ell}|L_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{i}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|Q_{l}e^{-\Delta\ell}\bar{Q}_{r}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle=-\frac{i}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|i\Delta e^{-\ell\Delta}\left(e^{-\frac{\ell}{2}-ia}-i\Delta\psi_{l}\bar{\psi}_{r}\right)|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\Delta}{\pi\sqrt{EE^{\prime}}}\langle F^{+}_{s^{\prime},j^{\prime}}|e^{-\ell(\Delta+\frac{1}{2})-ia}|F^{+}_{s,j}\rangle \displaystyle={\Delta\over\pi}\frac{\Gamma(\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\pm is\pm is^{\prime})}{\Gamma(2\Delta+1)}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-1}={1\over\pi}\frac{\Gamma(\Delta+\frac{1}{2}\pm is\pm is^{\prime})}{\Gamma(2\Delta)}\delta_{j^{\prime},j-1} $$

### F.1 Zero energy wavefunctions of the boundary particle

Here we look at the zero energy wavefunctions for the ${\cal N}=2$ problem. We solve for the functions now of one boundary particle that satisfy

$$ Q\Psi=\bar{Q}\Psi=0 $$

These wavefunctions are functions of $\gamma,\rho,x,a,\theta_{-},\bar{\theta}_{-},\chi$ . We work the reduced formalism of section 4.3.2. These functions are not invariant under the left $OSp(2|2)$ symmetries, but we do impose the right gauge symmetries. We will require that they transform in a definite way under ${\cal J}^{R}$ . Since $Q,\bar{Q}$ has $OSp(2|2)$ symmetry, the zero energy states must form a representation of this symmetry group.

We can furthermore diagonalize the left generator $\mathcal{L}_{-}$ to obtain

$$ \Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j}=e^{-\mathfrak{q}\gamma+ikx+ija}\left[e^{-ia/2}F(\rho,\theta_{-},\bar{\theta}_{-})+e^{ia/2}\chi\tilde{F}(\rho,\theta_{-},\bar{\theta}_{-})\right] $$

Note that in our notation $j-{1\over 2}$ corresponds to the right $R$ charge of the wavefunction. Note that on these functions $\mathcal{G}_{-}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{-}$ act essentially as complex fermion. Of course, these commute with $Q$ . So it is convenient to split the solutions into two possibilities obeying

$$ \bar{\mathcal{G}}_{-}\Psi_{+}=0~,~~~~~~~~~~~\mathcal{G}_{-}\Psi_{-}=0 $$

Of course, due to the anticommutation relations we get that $\mathcal{G}_{-}\Psi_{+}\propto\Psi_{-}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{G}}_{-}\Psi_{-}\propto\Psi_{+}$ . Solving these equations we find

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{+} \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-\mathfrak{q}\gamma+ikx+ija}e^{-\rho/2}\left[e^{-ia/2}(1-ik\theta_{-}\bar{\theta}_{-})K_{{1\over 2}+j}(v)-2e^{ia/2}\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}}\chi\theta_{-}K_{{1\over 2}-j}(v)\right] \displaystyle\Psi_{-} \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-\mathfrak{q}\gamma+ikx+ija}e^{-\rho/2}\left[-e^{-ia/2}{\bar{\theta}_{-}\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}}\over\mathfrak{q}}K_{{1\over 2}+j}(v)+e^{ia/2}\chi(1+ik\theta_{-}\bar{\theta}_{-})K_{{1\over 2}-j}(v)\right]~~~~~~ \displaystyle v\equiv 2e^{-\rho/2}\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}} $$

where each is defined up to a normalization. Note that the wavefunction with opposite $\mathfrak{q}$ and $k$ can be obained from these by simply taking $k\to-k$ and $\mathfrak{q}\to-\mathfrak{q}$ , which leaves $v$ invariant. Also note that $\Psi_{+}$ is Grassmann-even and $\Psi_{-}$ Grassmann-odd. The fact that there is a unique solution implies that there is a single zero energy solution for each $j$ and $k$ . In writing these wavefunctions we have picked the solution of the equations that is normalizable when $\rho\to-\infty$ . These wavefunctions are localized in the radial $\rho$ direction.

One of the lessons of this analysis is that, for each $j={\cal J}^{R}$ , there is a single irreducible representation in the zero-energy representation.

So, when we Fourier transform the propagator, we expect to find an answer which involves these functions. One question is: what is the inner product among these functions? The inner product can be computed with the measure in (144) involves

$$ \displaystyle\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{-}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bar{\theta}_{-}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\chi\,\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,+}\Psi_{-\mathfrak{q},-k,-j,-}\propto-2ik{1\over\cos\pi j} \displaystyle\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\rho\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta_{-}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\bar{\theta}_{-}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\chi\,\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,-}\Psi_{-\mathfrak{q},-k,-j,+}\propto 2ik{1\over\cos\pi j} $$

These wavefunctions were computed in Euclidean space, so they are appropriate for the description of the Fourier transform of the propagator. It is also interesting to discuss the wavefunction in Lorentzian signature. In that case we simply change $x\to-it$ , $k\to-i\omega$ , so that the time dependence is now $e^{-i\omega t}$ . Then the variable $v$ becomes $v=2e^{-\rho/2}\sqrt{\omega\mathfrak{q}}$ . These are normalizable wavefunctions.

Note also that if we set $\theta_{-}=\bar{\theta}_{-}=0$ the functions become

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,+} \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-\mathfrak{q}\gamma+ikx+ija}e^{-\rho/2}\left[e^{-ia/2}K_{{1\over 2}+j}(v)\right] \displaystyle\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,-} \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-\mathfrak{q}\gamma+ikx+ija}e^{-\rho/2}\left[e^{ia/2}\chi K_{{1\over 2}-j}(v)\right]~~~~~~ \displaystyle v\equiv 2e^{-\rho/2}\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}} $$

where the dependence on $\chi$ appears in only one of the terms.

### F.2 Checking the composition law for general $j$

The propagator (142) has two terms, one involves $\chi_{1}$ and the other $\chi_{2}$ . Therefore we expect that the propagator has the structure

$$ \hat{P}\sim\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}k\left[\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,+}(1)\Psi_{-\mathfrak{q},-k,-j,-}(2)~\pm~\Psi_{\mathfrak{q},k,j,-}(1)\Psi_{-\mathfrak{q},-k,-j,+}(2)\right] $$

where we have not worked out the precise signs and factors. The Fourier transform of the functions appearing in the propagator can be computed at zero $\theta_{-}$ $\bar{\theta}_{-}$ .

Note that [11]

$$ I=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}xe^{-ikx}{\mathfrak{q}\sqrt{z_{1}z_{2}}\over x}e^{-\mathfrak{q}{z_{1}+z_{2}\over x}}K_{\nu}({2\mathfrak{q}\sqrt{z_{1}z_{2}}\over x})=2\mathfrak{q}\sqrt{z_{1}z_{2}}K_{\nu}(2\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{1}})K_{\nu}(2\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{2}}) $$

$$ I={2\over ik}[\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{1}}K_{\nu}(2\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{1}})][\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{2}}K_{\nu}(2\sqrt{ik\mathfrak{q}z_{2}})] $$

The extra factor of $k$ seems consistent with the extra $k$ in the inner product, in the sense that it would cancel the extra $k$ in the inner products (295), (296).

The simple $j$ dependence in the inner products (295) (296) is also saying that the composition law works for any $j$ as is works for $j=0$ , once we put the extra factor of $\cos\pi j$ in the propagator as in (147). So the check of the composition law for general $j$ is now complete. Namely, we first checked it for $j=0$ in position space. Then for general $j$ we go to Fourier space and we use the wavefunctions discussed above. We do not have to work out the precise signs and factors of $k$ because we already know that they work out for $j=0$ . So, all we need to check is the $j$ dependence of the inner products.

## Appendix G Extra zero modes for small $N$

Here we discuss the zero modes of the operator $\psi_{1}\bar{\psi}_{2}$ , projected into the zero eigenstate sector.

For even $N$ , we find that the number of zero modes is

$$ \begin{split}\text{number of zero modes}&=D(N,j,\hat{q})-{N-2\choose N/2+j-1}\\
&=D(N,j,\hat{q})-{N-2\choose\frac{1}{2}(N-2)+j}\end{split} $$

Here $D(N,j,\hat{q})$ is the number of ground states with charge $j$ . For $j=0,\hat{q}=3,D=2\times 3^{N/2-1}$ . This formula is valid if the above quantity is positive. If the above quantity is negative, there are no zero modes. Note that $D$ grows more slowly than $N\choose N/2$ , so at large $N$ there are no degeneracies. To obtain this formula, consider starting with a ground state and acting with $\bar{\psi}$ . This gives a state with charge $j-1$ . In general, this state is not a ground state, so we count the number of UV states with charge $j-1$ , which would be ${N\choose N/2+j-1}$ . If this Hilbert space is smaller than the Hilbert space of ground states, we will get some degeneracies. So the naive number of zero modes would be the difference in the dimensions:

$$ \begin{split}\text{naive number of zero modes}=D_{IR}-D_{UV}=D(N,j,\hat{q})-{N\choose N/2+j-1}\end{split} $$

This counting is not quite right because $\bar{\psi}_{2}$ even as a UV operator has a kernel, e.g., states where a $\bar{\psi}_{2}\ket{0}$ . So when counting the UV dimension, we should only count states that are in the image of $\bar{\psi}_{2}$ and are not in the kernel of $\psi_{1}$ . This constraint reduces the effective number of spins from $N\to N-2$ in the second term of (304), leading to (303).

We can obtain a formula for the number of ground states by fourier transforming the refined index:

$$ \begin{split}D(N,j,\hat{q})=\frac{1}{\hat{q}}\sum_{l=0}^{(\hat{q}-3)/2}2\cos\left(\frac{\pi j(1+2l)}{\hat{q}}\right)\left[2\cos\frac{\pi}{2q}(1+2l)\right]^{N}\end{split} $$

We numerically tested (303) for several small values of $N$ and $\hat{q}$ .

## Appendix H Schwarzian coefficient at large $q$

In the large $\hat{q}$ $\mathcal{N}=1$ SYK model, the Schwarzian coefficient is

$$ \begin{split}C_{\mathcal{N}=1}=\frac{N}{16\hat{q}^{2}\mathcal{J}}\end{split} $$

This can be read off from the thermodynamics computed in [12]. In the $\mathcal{N}=2$ model, the equations of motion are the complexified version of the equations of motion of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ model. This implies that the Schwarzian coefficient for $\mathcal{N}=2$ is simply twice that of the $\mathcal{N}=1$ model (for any choice of $\hat{q}$ ).

$$ \begin{split}C_{\mathcal{N}=2}=\frac{N}{8\hat{q}^{2}\mathcal{J}}\end{split} $$

If this is the case, extrapolating to $q=3$ , we get a prediction $\alpha_{s}\approx N/(108J)$ , with $\mathcal{J}=3J/2$ . This is close to the answer [30] obtained by numerically solving the large $N$ equations $\alpha_{s}=0.00842N/J$ .

## Appendix I Computation of the disk partition function from the 2-sided Liouville quantum mechanics

*Figure 19: We can view the disk partition function with total length $u_{1}+u_{2}=\beta$ as an amplitude in the 2-sided Liouville theory $\bra{\ell_c}e^{-\beta H}\ket{\ell_c}$ , where the proper length of the geodesic on the top and bottom are going to zero. This implies that the renormalized length $\ell_{c}\to-\infty$ . In this limit, the red curves disappear completely.*

One question is whether we can reproduce the disk density of states using the Liouville quantum mechanics. This is not obvious because the density of states is a 1-sided quantity, whereas the Hilbert space of Liouville quantum mechanics is associated to the 2-sided theory. The idea is to compute the partition function of the thermal circle with total length $\beta$ . We can arbitrarily divide the circle into a left side and right side. The two sides meet at two points, with the condition that the total length of the circle is $\beta$ , see Figure (19). Then the proposal is that

$$ \begin{split}Z(\beta)\propto\lim_{\ell_{c}\to-\infty}\bra{\ell_c}e^{-\beta H_{\text{Liouville}}}\ket{\ell_c}\end{split} $$

where $\ket{\ell_c}$ is a position eigenstate. We are imposing that the renormalized length goes to $-\infty$ at two points in the Euclidean past and future. (This is because the length is going to zero). Now we can write this in terms of the energy eigenfunctions

$$ \begin{split}Z(\beta)\propto\int\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}s|\psi_{s}(\ell_{c})|^{2}e^{-\beta s^{2}}.\end{split} $$

Here $\psi_{s}(\ell)$ is an energy eigenstate with energy $s^{2}$ with the scattering normalization that is natural to the 2-sided problem (see, e.g., equation 3.4 of [26]):

$$ \begin{split}\psi_{s}(\ell_{c})=\frac{2^{1-2is}}{\Gamma(-2is)}K_{2is}(4e^{-\ell_{c}/2}).\end{split} $$

The flat measure $ds$ is natural if we think of $s$ as the momentum of the incoming wave. Now notice that at large $\ell$ , the Bessel function decays to zero, but in a way that is independent of the energy, e.g., $K_{\alpha}(z)\sim e^{-z}\sqrt{\pi/(2z)}$ . Hence we get $|\psi_{s}(\ell)|^{2}\propto s\sinh(2 \pi s)$ . This gives the expected density of states $\rho(E)\propto\sinh(2 \pi\sqrt{E})$ . The overall normalization $\sim e^{S_{0}}$ is not determined in this method.

This works similarly in the $\mathcal{N}=2$ Liouville case, where the eigenfunctions are also Bessel functions. In this case the boundary condition should be $\ket{\ell_c, a=0}$ . (Since the length of the segment is going to zero, the holonomy between the two sides should also go to zero if the gauge field is continuous.) In addition, we choose

$$ \begin{split}(\psi_{l}+i\psi_{r})\ket{\ell_c,a=0}=(\bar{\psi}_{l}+i\bar{\psi}_{r})\ket{\ell_c,a=0}=0\end{split} $$

This is the natural condition for fermions in the infinite temperature TFD. Notice that as $\ell_{c}\to\infty$ , we have that the second term in the supercharges (8) dominates (assuming that we regulate the position eigenstates by a small amount of smearing independent of $\ell_{c}$ ):

$$ \displaystyle Q_{r} \displaystyle= \displaystyle e^{-\ell_{c}/2}\psi_{l}~,~~~~~~~\bar{Q}_{r}=e^{-\ell_{c}/2}\bar{\psi}_{l} \displaystyle Q_{l} \displaystyle= \displaystyle-e^{-\ell_{c}/2-ia}\psi_{r}~,~~~~~~~\bar{Q}_{l}=-e^{-\ell_{c}/2}\bar{\psi}_{r}~~~~ $$

Therefore this state satisfies

$$ \begin{split}(Q_{r}-iQ_{\ell})\ket{\ell_c, a=0}=(\bar{Q}_{r}-i\bar{Q}_{\ell})\ket{\ell_c, a=0}=0.\end{split} $$

Since the supercharges commute with the Hamiltonian, this must be true for the $\ket{\tfd}$ state at finite $\beta$ :

$$ \begin{split}\ket{\tfd}=e^{-\beta H/2}\ket{\ell_c, a=0}.\quad\end{split} $$

This provides a derivation of the equation

$$ (Q_{r}-iQ_{\ell})|\mathrm{TFD}\rangle=(\bar{Q}_{r}-i\bar{Q}_{\ell})|\mathrm{TFD}\rangle=0 $$

Note that this method also generalizes to the disk with a finite chemical potential, by inserting $e^{-\mu Q}$ , which can be achieved by acting with $e^{-\mu J}$ in the 2-sided theory. In this way, we can read off the density of states for each charge sector $j$ .

The following comment is an aside. Note that we could imagine evaluating $\bra{\ell_c}e^{-\beta H_{\text{Liouville}}}\ket{\ell_c}$ via saddle point. The saddle point solutions are

$$ \begin{split}e^{-\ell}={\sin^{-2}(\pi u/\beta)},\quad a=2\pi n\hat{q}(u/\beta)\end{split} $$

Since the partition function is 1-loop exact, this implies that the saddle-point approximation in the Liouville theory is 1-loop exact in the limit of large $\ell_{c}$ . It would be interesting to explain the 1-loop exactness in the context of Liouville quantum mechanics.

## Appendix J Simplifying the “phase” factors

In this subsection we will consider the bosonic case and simplify the expression of the phase factors that appears in the chain of propagators dressing a diagram. These involve the combination

$$ \varphi_{12}+\varphi_{23}+\varphi_{34}+\cdots\varphi_{n1}~,~~~~~{\rm with}~~~~\varphi_{ij}={e^{-\rho_{i}}+e^{-\rho_{j}}\over x_{i}-x_{j}} $$

see (99). This does not involves the variables $\gamma_{i}$ so we expect that they could be expressed in terms of the distance variables. In fact, it is relatively easy to do that. First we note that a given $\rho_{i}$ appears in just two terms $\varphi_{i-1,i}$ and $\varphi_{i,i+1}$ and these two combine into

$$ e^{-\rho_{i}}{x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}\over(x_{i}-x_{i-1})(x_{i+1}-x_{i})}=\exp\left(-{\ell_{i,i+1}\over 2}-{\ell_{i,i-1}\over 2}+{\ell_{i-1,i+1}\over 2}\right) $$

where the total argument of the exponent in the right hand side is always negative due to the triangle inequality for distances. Some care is needed for the last term involving $\varphi_{n1}$ , but in the end the formula is also valid for that case.

So the conclusion is that the final phase factor terms have the form

$$ \prod_{i}e^{-\varphi_{i,i+1}}=\exp\left(-\sum_{i}e^{-{\ell_{i,i+1}\over 2}-{\ell_{i,i-1}\over 2}+{\ell_{i-1,i+1}\over 2}}\right) $$

In particular, only the lengths between nearest neighbors and next-to-nearest neighbors appear. For the supersymmetric case, we expect a similar simplification.

## Appendix K Relative entropy

An interesting question is whether there is any notion of the entanglement wedge of a subregion in the extremal regime, where the boundary mode is highly quantum. Here a subregion could just be one side of the 2-sided wormhole. To address this question, we compute the relative entropy of different density matrices $\rho,\sigma$ which are obtained by tracing out one side of the wormhole. By inserting different types of matter in the middle of the wormhole, one could diagnose our ability to do 1-sided bulk reconstruction. To compute the relative entropy, we can use the replica trick:

$$ \begin{split}S(\rho\mid\sigma)=\left.-\partial_{n}\tr\left(\rho\sigma^{n-1}-\rho^{n}\right)\right|_{n=1}\end{split} $$

If we take $\rho$ to be the maximally mixed state (e.g. the empty wormhole) and $\sigma$ to be 1-sided density matrix of a wormhole with $q$ identical light particles with $\Delta=0$ , we get (compare with (184)):

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{n\to 1}\frac{1}{1-n}\left((2q(n-1)-1)!!-1\right)=\psi^{(0)}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\log(2)=q\times(1.270\dots)\end{split} $$

where the analytic continuation of the double factorial is as in (184).

For $q$ heavy particles $\Delta\gg 1$ , we also get a relative entropy that grows linearly with $q$ :

$$ \begin{split}-\partial_{n}\left.\left[\frac{(2q(n-1))!}{(q(n-1)+1)!(q(n-1))!}-1\right]\right|_{n=1}=q.\end{split} $$

In the above calculations we are asking whether we can distinguish the empty wormhole from the case for a wormhole with matter. Another question more closely related to the standard bulk reconstruction question is whether we can distinguish a wormhole with a qubit in the state $\ket{\uparrow}$ from a wormhole with a qubit in the state $\ket{\downarrow}$ . To model this, we can consider 2 species of particles, both with the same dimension. For $\Delta=0$ , we get

$$ \begin{split}\lim_{n\to 1}\frac{1}{1-n}\left((2(n-1)-1)!!-(2n-1)!!\right)=2\end{split} $$

This says that we can recover some partial information about the state of the probe qubit. Of course, we cannot recover the state exactly or else we would violate cloning.

An interesting setup for future work is to consider with $K$ particle insertions, all separated by infinite Euclidean time evolution. The state of $K-1$ of the $K$ particles are fixed, but one of the $K$ particles is treated as the probe qubit, the state of which we would like to reconstruct. In this setup, it would be interesting to study the relative entropy as a function of which of the $K$ particles we choose to have an unknown state. The semiclassical picture would suggest that if the probe qubit is to the left of the midpoint of the wormhole, the corresponding relative entropy of the left boundary would be large, whereas if the probe qubit is to the right of the midpoint, the relative entropy should be small. It would be interesting to do this computation at large $\Delta\gg 1$ ; for $\Delta=0$ we note that we just have Wick contractions so there is no difference in which order we put the particles.
